mcqs.q: A radiograph should be made:
opts: Only after a thorough history and clinical examination, tailored to the patient
Routinely for every patient before examination
mcqs.explain: Imaging is performed only after a medical/dental history and clinical exam, tailored to the patient's needs and the diagnostic task.

mcqs.q: The overriding principle for taking any radiograph is that:
opts: The diagnostic/treatment benefit outweighs the radiation risk
More images always give better care
Radiation has no risk at diagnostic doses
mcqs.explain: A radiograph is justified only when the potential diagnostic and treatment benefit outweighs the radiation risk to the patient.

mcqs.q: Choosing which radiograph to take depends on all EXCEPT:
opts: The technique's sensitivity, specificity and resolution
mcqs.explain: The choice depends on the abnormality's nature/severity, the technique's sensitivity/specificity, the resolution required, and the radiation dose — not on appointment timing.

mcqs.q: Intra-oral radiographs are preferred for teeth because they have:
mcqs.explain: Intra-oral images give the highest spatial resolution, ideal for teeth and their supporting structures.

mcqs.q: A noted limitation of periapical (IOPA) imaging is:
mcqs.explain: Although the IOPA optimally shows the root and supporting structures, its limitation is geometric distortion.

mcqs.q: The bitewing radiograph is OPTIMAL for revealing:
opts: Interproximal caries and crestal bone levels
mcqs.explain: A bitewing places the receptor against the crowns of a sextant and the alveolar crests, making it optimal for interproximal caries.

mcqs.q: An occlusal radiograph is useful because it:
opts: Images larger areas of the jaws without compromising resolution
Has the lowest resolution of all views
mcqs.explain: Occlusal images supplement periapical/bitewing views and cover larger areas of the jaws while keeping good resolution.

mcqs.q: Compared with intra-oral images, panoramic radiography offers:
opts: A broad view of the jaws but lower spatial resolution
mcqs.explain: Panoramic imaging gives a broad view of the midface and jaws, but with lower resolution, distortion, superimposition and motion artifacts.

mcqs.q: Advanced imaging (CBCT, CT, MRI) should be ordered:
opts: Only if intra-oral or panoramic imaging does not provide the needed information, and referred to a radiologist
mcqs.explain: Advanced modalities are reserved for when intra-oral/panoramic imaging is insufficient; these procedures should be referred to a radiologist.

mcqs.q: Which statement about CT and MRI is correct?
opts: CT shows cross-sectional anatomy/bone (high dose); MRI is non-ionizing and shows soft tissue
MRI uses a high radiation dose; CT is non-ionizing
mcqs.explain: CT gives cross-sectional anatomy and bone pathology at a high dose; MRI is non-ionizing and excels at soft tissue.

mcqs.q: It is considered INAPPROPRIATE to:
opts: Irradiate a patient 'just to see if there is something there'
Take a radiograph when clinical signs suggest disease
Compare with a patient's previous images
Use bitewings to detect interproximal caries
mcqs.explain: Radiographs must be justified; it is inappropriate to irradiate 'just to see if there is something there.'

mcqs.q: An accepted EXCEPTION to imaging only when clinical signs exist is:
opts: Bitewing images to detect interproximal caries even with no clinical signs
Full-mouth series for every new patient
mcqs.explain: Bitewings for early interproximal caries are an accepted exception, since such caries may not be clinically evident.

mcqs.q: For a cooperative CHILD in the PRIMARY dentition with closed posterior contacts, the recommended initial imaging is:
mcqs.explain: With closed contacts, only bitewings are needed to detect interproximal caries; open contacts may need none.

mcqs.q: For a child in the MIXED dentition (after the first permanent molar erupts), guidelines recommend:
opts: Bitewings plus a panoramic or selected periapical/occlusal images
mcqs.explain: Mixed dentition: bitewings for caries plus a panoramic (or selected PA/occlusal) to detect growth-and-development abnormalities.

mcqs.q: A dentate adult with WIDESPREAD caries or periodontal disease may require:
opts: A full-mouth series of periapical and bitewing images
mcqs.explain: Generalized disease may justify a full-mouth series; if disease is localized, a limited subset suffices.

mcqs.q: For a HIGH-risk/clinically-evident-caries ADULT, the recommended bitewing recall interval is:
mcqs.explain: High-risk adults: 6–18 months. Low-risk adults extend to 24–36 months.

mcqs.q: For a LOW-risk CHILD, the recommended caries-recall bitewing interval is:
mcqs.explain: Low-risk children: 12–24 months; low-risk adolescents 18–36 months; low-risk adults 24–36 months.

mcqs.q: To establish and monitor periodontal bone loss, the appropriate images are:
opts: A combination of periapical and bitewing images
mcqs.explain: Periodontal assessment generally uses intra-oral periapical and bitewing images to establish and monitor bone-loss severity.

mcqs.q: Reviewing a new patient's PREVIOUS radiographs is important because they:
opts: Allow comparison with the current image, regardless of when they were made
Replace the need for a clinical examination
Are only useful if less than 1 month old
mcqs.explain: Prior images, whenever made, are valuable for comparison; the dentist should review and try to obtain them for every new patient.

mcqs.q: 'Administrative' radiographs taken only to satisfy an insurance company:
opts: Typically do not benefit the patient
mcqs.explain: Administrative images (e.g. for insurance approval) typically do not benefit the patient and should be weighed against the radiation risk.

mcqs.q: Which patient groups warrant SPECIAL consideration before imaging?
opts: Pregnant patients and those on radiation therapy
mcqs.explain: Pregnancy and radiation therapy are special considerations requiring extra caution and individualized decisions.

mcqs.q: Which is the FIRST step before any radiographic prescription?
opts: Choosing a CBCT field of view
mcqs.explain: A thorough history and clinical examination always precede and guide the decision to image.

saqs.q: State the principles governing WHEN to take a radiograph.
saqs.a: Only after history & clinical examination, tailored to the patient's needs/task, and only when the benefit outweighs the radiation risk.

saqs.q: On what four factors does the choice of radiological examination depend?
saqs.a: Nature/severity of the abnormality, the technique's sensitivity/specificity, the resolution needed, and the radiation dose.

saqs.q: Compare intra-oral and panoramic imaging in terms of resolution and coverage.
saqs.a: Intra-oral: highest resolution, small coverage (teeth/support). Panoramic: broad coverage of the jaws but lower resolution, with distortion/superimposition.

saqs.q: When should advanced imaging (CBCT/CT/MRI) be used, and what does each provide?
saqs.a: Only when intra-oral/panoramic is insufficient (refer to a radiologist). CT = cross-sectional bone (high dose); MRI = non-ionizing soft tissue.

saqs.q: Give the imaging recommendation for a child in the mixed dentition.
saqs.a: Bitewings for interproximal caries plus a panoramic (or selected PA/occlusal) to detect growth-and-development abnormalities.

saqs.q: State the caries-recall bitewing intervals for high-risk vs low-risk adults.
Why is it wrong to image 'just to see', and what is the one exception?
saqs.a: Every exposure must be justified (benefit > risk); irradiating 'just to see' is inappropriate. Exception: bitewings for interproximal caries even without clinical signs.
